summary: Gives guidelines for planning fully online meetings, including the number, length, and composition of sessions on the agenda. It is based on experience from IETF online meetings during the COVID-19 pandemic.

plainLanguage.summary: Tips for running a big meeting over video: how many sessions, how long, and who should be in each.

questions: how to organize a fully online meeting
how to schedule global meetings across time zones
subtitle: How to organize large engineering meetings entirely online: timing, duration, and structure.

tldr.problem: When the IETF moved to fully online meetings during the COVID-19 pandemic, organizers had to figure out how many sessions per day, how long each should be, and what time of day works for a global audience scattered across time zones.
tldr.mechanism: The solution rotates meeting times between three time slots so that no region is always inconvenienced. Sessions last 5 to 6 hours per day over 5 days, with 60-minute or 120-minute sessions separated by 30-minute breaks.
tldr.outcome: Participant surveys showed satisfaction with the structure. Online meetings can be as productive as in-person ones if the format accounts for the fatigue of remote participation and gives time for the informal networking that happens in hallways.

today: RFC 9400 is an Informational document describing lessons learned from 2020–2021 online IETF meetings. It has not been obsoleted and remains the current guidance for organizing large online meetings.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
When COVID-19 shut down travel in March 2020, the IETF had two weeks to convert its plenary meeting to a fully online event. Over 2020 and 2021, the IETF held multiple online meetings and gathered feedback on what worked and what did not.

This RFC captures those lessons: how to choose meeting times to be fair to global participants, how long each day should be, how to structure sessions and breaks, and how many parallel tracks are practical. The guidance is based on post-meeting surveys from thousands of participants.

Remote participation is more tiring than in-person attendance. Smaller session lists and longer breaks proved important for maintaining engagement.
sections.plainLanguage: During the pandemic, the IETF ran big meetings online. This explains what schedules worked best.

sections.title: Time Zone Selection
sections.content:
A global meeting must hold some sessions at inconvenient times for someone. The RFC proposes rotating between three time windows so that over three meetings, most participants get one meeting at a reasonable hour in the morning or evening, and only one in the middle of the night.

The three time slots are calibrated to daylight-saving transitions:

North America Night: 0500–1100 UTC (roughly morning in North America, evening in Europe, middle of day in Asia).

Asia Night: 1300–1900 UTC (roughly evening in Asia, night in Europe, early morning in North America).

Europe Night: 2200–0400 UTC (roughly evening in Europe, middle of night in Asia, early morning in North America).

By rotating the meeting time among these three slots across consecutive meetings, the burden is distributed fairly and predictably.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of always picking a time that is bad for one part of the world, rotate the meeting time so everyone gets a fair turn having it at a decent hour.

sections.title: Duration and Session Structure
sections.content:
Early online meetings used either a reduced agenda (two 4-hour days) or a full agenda (eight to nine parallel tracks like an in-person meeting). Surveys showed strong preference (82%) for a full agenda compressed into 5 days.

The sweet spot is 5 to 6 hours of meetings per day over 5 days. Remote participation is more cognitively tiring than in-person meeting attendance, so participants fatigue faster. In-person meetings can run 8 or more hours; online meetings top out at 6 before quality drops.

Each meeting day includes two to three 60-minute or 120-minute sessions with 30-minute breaks between them. The longer breaks (vs. the 10 minutes used in-person) give time for meals, exercise, and informal hallway conversations using online tools like video breakout rooms.
sections.plainLanguage: A 5-day week, 6 hours a day, with sessions that last 60 or 120 minutes and half-hour breaks is what works best online.

sections.title: Parallel Tracks and Scheduling
sections.content:
In-person meetings have at most 8 or 9 parallel tracks because of room availability. Online meetings are not constrained by physical space, so technically they could have more tracks. However, more tracks mean more scheduling conflicts for participants who want to attend multiple sessions.

The IETF 111 experiment with 9 parallel tracks showed no statistically significant increase in dissatisfaction about conflicts. So 8 to 9 tracks remain practical.

If demand for sessions exceeds capacity, working group chairs are encouraged to use interim meetings between plenary meetings for focused work, rather than bloating the main meeting with too many sessions. This spreads load over time and lets focused groups meet at more convenient times.
sections.plainLanguage: Eight or nine sessions can run at the same time without making it hard for people to pick what to watch. More sessions means more choices but also more conflicts.

sections.title: Participation and Challenges
sections.content:
Online meetings showed more consistent geographic participation than in-person meetings. Time zones were rotated, and participation from less common regions remained stable across meetings, showing that online formats remove the travel burden that favors participants in wealthy, well-connected regions.

However, online meetings lack informal hallway conversations. Despite investments in virtual breakout spaces, many participants did not use them, preferring meals, sleep, and rest. This loss of serendipitous collaboration may explain a slight decrease in new Internet-Draft submissions during 2020–2021, even as overall submissions remained stable.

The RFC recommends continued experimentation with structure and timing to optimize both formal sessions and informal networking opportunities in a remote setting.
sections.plainLanguage: Online meetings let people from far away join more easily. But they miss the casual conversations that happen in hallways, which can inspire new ideas.
